title: Classifying costs without mixing the questions

blocks.heading: Classifying costs without mixing the questions
blocks.text: Fixed and variable classify cost behaviour as output changes in the relevant period. Fixed total cost does not vary with output within the stated range; total variable cost changes with output. Direct and indirect classify whether a cost can be traced to a particular product or department. A direct cost is identifiable with that cost object; an indirect cost, or overhead, is shared and cannot be directly traced to it. In simple examples direct materials are variable and rent is fixed overhead, but the two pairs answer different questions and are not universal synonyms. Unit or average cost divides total cost by total output. Marginal cost is the extra cost from producing one more unit. Total cost is the full amount for the stated output, not an amount per item. Each measure has a purpose: a manager comparing total expenditure needs total cost, whereas pricing or efficiency comparisons may require unit cost. State the output and time period so that two figures are comparable.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Rani Crates has monthly rent N$2,000 and timber costing N$30 per crate. At 100 crates, assume these are its complete production costs. Rent is fixed over the stated output range; timber is variable and traceable to crates. Total cost is N$5,000 and average cost is N$50 per crate. One extra crate costs N$30 if no extra fixed cost arises, so marginal cost is N$30, distinct from average cost.

blocks.heading: Fixed costs
blocks.text: Fixed costs do not vary with the items produced or sold in the short term within the stated operating range. Rent is a common example. The total stays fixed as output changes over that range, but fixed cost per unit falls as the same amount is spread over more units. Beyond the range, extra premises or machinery can change total fixed cost. Fixed describes behaviour, not whether a cost can be traced to a product.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Oru Packs pays rent N$3,000 per month whether it makes 100 or 150 packs. The total rent remains N$3,000. Rent per pack falls from N$30 to N$20 across those outputs; a fixed total is not a fixed cost per item.

blocks.heading: Variable costs
blocks.text: Variable costs change in total as output changes. In a simple constant-rate model, each extra item requires a given amount of material, so total material cost rises with the number produced while cost per item stays constant. A changing input price or wastage rate can alter this relationship, so state the model assumptions. Variable is distinct from direct, which concerns traceability to a product or department.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Iwa Bags uses N$12 fabric per bag and makes 100 bags, then 150, with no price or usage change. Fabric cost rises from N$1,200 to N$1,800 while remaining N$12 per bag. The total changes with output; it is not a fixed N$12 bill for the business.

blocks.heading: Direct costs
blocks.text: Direct costs are costs that can be directly related to or identified with a particular product or department. Direct material is a simple example. The key is traceability: ask which product or department caused the cost and whether it can be identified without a shared allocation. Direct materials often vary with output, but direct/indirect and fixed/variable are different classifications. A fixed hire payment for equipment used solely on one identified project can be direct to that project.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Lela Doors buys timber specifically for an identified door order. The timber can be traced to that order, making it direct to the order. Its variable behaviour is a separate description of how the amount changes with output.

blocks.heading: Indirect costs
blocks.text: An indirect cost is a cost which cannot be directly related to a particular product. Such costs are often called overhead costs. Shared factory rent is indirect to individual product lines and may need allocation if managers want a full cost for each line. Indirect does not mean unnecessary. Many simple overheads are fixed, but an indirect cost can change with activity; the category concerns traceability, not an automatic fixed amount.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Tano Furnishings makes desks and chairs in one rented workshop, with no separate rented areas identified for each. The shared rent is indirect to the product lines. Charging its full amount to every desk and again to every chair would double count rather than allocate a shared cost.

blocks.heading: Unit costs
blocks.text: Unit cost is the cost of producing one item, i.e. total cost of production divided by total output. It expresses the average cost per item at the stated output, not necessarily the cost of the next extra item. Include the relevant full production costs in total cost and keep currency per unit distinct from a total money amount. Compare the same type and quality of output where possible.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Noa Trays has total production cost N$9,000 for 300 trays. Unit cost is N$30 per tray. N$9,000 is total cost, while N$30 is cost per item. That average alone does not establish the marginal cost of making tray 301.

blocks.heading: Average costs
blocks.text: Average cost is total cost divided by output. For a single type of product it is the same average-per-item concept as unit cost. It can change with the output level even when the marginal variable cost is constant, because fixed costs are spread over different quantities. Lower average cost with expansion requires relevant conditions, such as capacity use and controlled coordination costs; diseconomies can offset savings as the business grows.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Re-read after expressing percentage conversions explicitly and qualifying average-cost changes with capacity and coordination conditions; the unchanged numerical examples and comparisons still hold.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Kela Cups has total cost N$4,000 at 100 cups and N$5,000 at 200 cups. Average cost falls from N$40 per cup to N$25 per cup. The increase in total cost is N$1,000 over 100 extra cups, which is different from either average figure.

blocks.heading: Marginal costs
blocks.text: Marginal costs are extra costs which a business will incur by producing one more unit of output. If output increases by several units, the change in total cost divided by the output change gives the average additional cost over that interval; it equals the per-extra-unit marginal cost only under the stated constant-increment assumption. Marginal cost is useful for examining an additional unit but does not by itself recover the business’s full fixed commitments.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Teta Tiles has total cost N$8,000 at 200 tiles and N$8,025 at 201 tiles. The extra tile adds N$25, so its marginal cost is N$25. Average cost at 200 tiles is N$40; the marginal and average figures answer different questions.

blocks.heading: Total costs
blocks.text: Total cost is the full cost of producing the stated output over a period. In the simple fixed-and-variable model it is total fixed cost plus total variable cost. Do not add a per-unit variable cost directly to a total fixed-cost bill: first multiply the per-unit amount by output. Total cost carries a money unit, whereas average and marginal cost carry money per item. Its completeness depends on which costs the situation includes.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Aro Boxes has fixed costs N$2,000 and variable cost N$10 per box for 300 boxes. Assume these are all its production costs. Total variable cost is N$3,000 and total cost N$5,000. The N$10 is an input rate per box, not the full variable bill or the total cost.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Financial evidence and judgement
blocks.text:
Fictional Ema Cabinets reports annual net profit N$30,000, capital employed N$150,000, total assets N$200,000 and total liabilities N$80,000. Its current ratio is 1.80:1 and quick ratio 0.90:1. A supplier is deciding whether to offer short credit. Debtors are currently expected to pay before the proposed supplier bill falls due. The owner is willing to share current cash-flow information. Ema has fixed workshop rent and timber costs that vary with output. For part (b) only, the largest debtor now says payment will arrive two months after the proposed supplier bill is due. All reported profit and asset figures remain unchanged.

a Evaluate whether Ema’s supplier should offer the proposed credit under the original facts. Use the ratios, relevant cost behaviour and the interests of different statement users. [12]
b Evaluate the credit decision after the debtor delay. Explain whether the earlier judgement changes. [12]

a Ema’s ROCE is 20.00% and solvency ratio 2.50:1, useful to an owner assessing return and a lender assessing total asset cover. A supplier needs short-term receipts: quick ratio 0.90:1 shows non-inventory coverage below current liabilities, but expected debtor receipts before the bill and an available current forecast can support a limited credit offer. Fixed rent and variable timber payments both compete for the receipts. Check the forecast, existing commitments and the individual due amounts, then offer a controlled limit if payment is credible; the annual profit alone cannot justify it. b The delayed largest receipt undermines the key cash-timing support while profit, ROCE and book asset cover remain unchanged. A future profitable result cannot pay the earlier bill without cash from another stated source. The supplier should now postpone or reduce credit, seek payment on delivery or require evidence of an agreed alternative cash source. This changes the original conditional willingness because receipt timing, rather than annual profitability, was decisive. Do not invent a new overdraft to preserve the original answer.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Financial evidence and judgement
blocks.text:
Fictional Ema Cabinets reports annual net profit N$30,000, capital employed N$150,000, total assets N$200,000 and total liabilities N$80,000. Its current ratio is 1.80:1 and quick ratio 0.90:1. A supplier is deciding whether to offer short credit. Debtors are currently expected to pay before the proposed supplier bill falls due. The owner is willing to share current cash-flow information. Ema has fixed workshop rent and timber costs that vary with output.

Evaluate whether Ema’s supplier should use profitability or liquidity evidence as its primary basis for the credit decision. Give a concise plan, including the owner’s different interest and one cost distinction. [12]

Knowledge: profit measures performance; liquidity concerns short-term payment; solvency compares total assets and total liabilities. ROCE is 30,000 / 150,000 × 100, giving 20.00%, relevant to an owner’s return but not sufficient for a supplier’s due date. Evidence: current ratio 1.80:1 falls to quick ratio 0.90:1, so part of coverage depends on inventory. Debtors are expected before the bill and the owner offers cash-flow evidence, which may support credit after verification. Costs: workshop rent is fixed in the stated range while timber varies with output; future payments for both still matter to cash. Judgement: prioritise current liquidity and cash timing for short credit, use profitability and asset cover as supporting evidence and verify the forecast. An owner may give return more weight, but cannot ignore liquidity that threatens continuity.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why average cost N$40 per pot is not the marginal cost of one extra pot. Fictional Yara Pots has total cost N$4,000 at 100 pots and N$4,025 at 101 pots.

Average cost at 100 pots divides total cost by output, giving N$40 per pot. The extra pot adds N$25 to total cost, so its marginal cost is N$25. Average includes the allocation of all costs across output; marginal focuses on the extra unit.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why fictional Rula Works’ rent is an expense but its net profit is not a type of fixed cost. Its rent is unchanged over the stated output range.

Rent is a cost charged against income and is fixed in the stated range because its total does not vary with output. Net profit is the residual after relevant costs and expenses are deducted from income. Income/expense describes financial performance categories; fixed/variable describes cost behaviour. A profit result cannot be reclassified as fixed merely because a rent bill is fixed.
